The 1964 version recorded by British singer [[Petula Clark]] became an international hit, reaching number one on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and number two on the UK Singles Chart. [[Tony Hatch]] first worked with Petula Clark when he assisted her producer [[Alan A. Freeman]] on her 1961 {{abbr|No.|Number}} 1 hit "[[Sailor (song)|Sailor]]". In 1963 Freeman asked Hatch to take over as Clark's regular producer. Hatch subsequently produced five English-language singles for Clark, none of which charted.

In late 1964 Hatch made his first visit to [[New York City]], spending three days there in search of material from music publishers for the artists he was producing. He recalled, "I was staying at a hotel on [[Central Park]] and I wandered down to [[Broadway (Manhattan)|Broadway]] and to [[Times Square]] and, naively, I thought I was downtown. ... I loved the whole atmosphere there and the [music] came to me very, very quickly".<ref name=retrosellers>{{cite web|url=http://www.retrosellers.com/features152.htm |title=Tony Hatch interview |publisher=Retrosellers.com |date=November 2007 |access-date=22 January 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303191002/http://www.retrosellers.com/features152.htm |archive-date=3 March 2016}}</ref> He was standing on the corner of [[List of numbered streets in Manhattan|48th Street]] in [[Midtown Manhattan|Midtown]], waiting for the traffic lights to change and looking towards Times Square when "the melody first came to me, just as the neon signs went on."<ref name="Going Back Downtown">{{cite news| url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424127887324866904578513153605764288 | title=Going Back Downtown| author=Marc Myers| website=The Wall Street Journal| date=12 June 2013 |access-date=22 January 2015}}</ref>

Hatch envisioned his embryonic composition "as a sort of [[doo-wop|doo wop]] [[rhythm and blues|R&B]] song", which he thought to eventually pitch to [[the Drifters]]:<ref name="Cold Pizza For Breakfast">{{cite book  | first=Christine  | last=Lavin  | year=2010  | title=Cold Pizza For Breakfast: a mem-wha??  | publisher=Tell Me Press  | location=New Haven, CT  | page=[https://archive.org/details/coldpizzaforbrea00lavi/page/218 218]  | isbn=978-0-9816453-6-0  | url-access=registration  | url=https://archive.org/details/coldpizzaforbrea00lavi/page/218  }}</ref> He had scored his biggest success to date with [[The Searchers (band)|the Searchers]]' "[[Sugar and Spice (The Searchers song)|Sugar and Spice]]" modelled on the Drifters' hit "[[Sweets for My Sweet]]", and had also produced a [[cover version]] of the Drifters' "[[Up on the Roof (song)|Up on the Roof]]" for [[Julie Grant]]. It has been said that Hatch gave Julie Grant the opportunity to record "Downtown" which Grant turned down,<ref name="AMG">{{cite web |url={{AllMusic|class=artist|id=p194551/biography|pure_url=yes}}|title=Julie Grant|author=Richie Unterberger |publisher=[[AllMusic]] |access-date=23 May 2013}}</ref> but this does not accord with Hatch's statement that he played "Downtown" for Petula Clark within a few days of conceiving the melody and only completed the song's lyrics after Clark had asked to record it. Hatch has also said that, before Clark expressed interest in "Downtown", "it never occurred to me that a white woman could even sing it."<ref name="Cold Pizza For Breakfast"/> Hatch has subsequently denied originally offering "Downtown" to the Drifters.<ref name=Hatch>{{cite news|author=Interviews by Dave Simpson |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2016/oct/11/petula-clark-tony-hatch-how-we-made-downtown |title=Petula Clark: how we made Downtown|newspaper=The Guardian |date= 11 October 2016|access-date=24 June 2017}}</ref>

Within a few days of his New York City trip Hatch visited Paris to present Clark with three or four songs he had acquired from New York publishers for Clark to consider recording at a London recording session scheduled for 16 October 1964, which was roughly two weeks away. Hatch said of the meeting: "She was not very enthusiastic about [the material] and asked me if I was working on anything new myself."<ref name="Daeida">''Daeida'' April 2010 p.2</ref> According to Clark, besides the title lyric, Hatch had only written "one or two lines."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.retrosellers.com/features149.htm |title=Petula Clark interview |publisher=Retrosellers.com |date=October 2007 |access-date=14 June 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140227171604/http://www.retrosellers.com/features149.htm |archive-date=27 February 2014}}</ref> Hatch recalled: "Reluctantly, I played her the tune of my New York inspiration and slipped in the word 'Downtown' in the appropriate places."<ref name="Daeida"/> Clark, who first heard "Downtown" from her kitchen, having stepped away to make a pot of tea, told Hatch: "That's the one I want to record."<ref name="Daeida"/> "Get that finished. Get a good lyric in it. Get a great arrangement and I think we'll at least have a song we're proud to record even if it isn't a hit."<ref name="Sound on Sound">{{cite web| url=http://www.soundonsound.com/sos/jan12/articles/classic-tracks-0112.htm| title=Petula Clark "Downtown" | work=Sound on Sound| access-date=12 July 2013}}</ref>

It has been said that Hatch gave Julie Grant the opportunity to record "Downtown" which Grant turned down, but this does not accord with Hatch's statement that he played "Downtown" for Petula Clark within a few days of conceiving the melody and only completed the song's lyrics after Clark had asked to record it. Hatch has also said that, before Clark expressed interest in "Downtown", "it never occurred to me that a white woman could even sing it." Hatch has subsequently denied originally offering "Downtown" to the Drifters.

Within a few days of his New York City trip Hatch visited Paris to present Clark with three or four songs he had acquired from New York publishers for Clark to consider recording at a London recording session scheduled for 16 October 1964, which was roughly two weeks away. Hatch said of the meeting: "She was not very enthusiastic about [the material] and asked me if I was working on anything new myself." According to Clark, besides the title lyric, Hatch had only written "one or two lines." Hatch recalled: "Reluctantly, I played her the tune of my New York inspiration and slipped in the word 'Downtown' in the appropriate places." Clark, who first heard "Downtown" from her kitchen, having stepped away to make a pot of tea, told Hatch: "That's the one I want to record." "Get that finished. Get a good lyric in it. Get a great arrangement and I think we'll at least have a song we're proud to record even if it isn't a hit."

sections.heading: Recording
sections.wikitext:
"Downtown" was recorded on 16 October 1964 at the Pye Studios in [[Marble Arch]]. Thirty minutes before the session was scheduled, Hatch was still touching up the song's lyrics in the studio's washroom. Hatch said of his arrangement: "I had to connect with young record buyers... but not alienate Pet[ula]'s older core audience... The trick was to make a giant orchestra sound like a rock band."<ref name="Going Back Downtown"/> Hatch insisted that all session personnel on his productions be recorded performing together. The session personnel for the recording of "Downtown" were assembled in Studio One of Pye Recording Studios and included eight violinists, two viola players and two cellists, four trumpeters and four trombonists, five woodwind players with flutes and oboes, percussionists, a bass player and a pianist.<ref name="Harrington p. 107">Harrington, Patrick and Bobby Graham, The Session Man; The story of Bobby Graham the UK’s greatest session drummer, Broom House, Monmouthshire, 2004 p. 107</ref>

Also playing on the session were guitarists [[Vic Flick]], [[Jimmy Page]] and [[Big Jim Sullivan]], as well as drummer [[Ronnie Verrell]], while [[the Breakaways]] provided the vocal accompaniment. [[Bobby Graham (musician)|Bobby Graham]] was also credited as drummer on the session.<ref name="Harrington p. 107"/> Brian Brocklehurst stated in 1995 that he played upright bass at the session. Hatch's assistant Bob Leaper conducted.<ref name="Sound on Sound"/> According to Petula Clark, the session for "Downtown" consisted of three [[Alternate takes|take]]s with the second take ultimately chosen as the completed track yet, elsewhere, an "extended" version consisting of an instrumental and backing vocal track most likely from a session tape, makes this claim questionable.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.northamptonchron.co.uk/what-s-on/theatre/star-interview-petula-clark-1-5327701| title=Star Interview: Petula Clark| publisher=Northamptonchron.co.uk| access-date=7 August 2013}}</ref>

sections.heading: Impact
sections.wikitext:
Tony Hatch would recall playing the completed "Downtown" track for [[Pye Records]] executives, saying: "Nobody knew what to make of it and no release date was set. Then Pye's general manager called and said Joe Smith – [[Warner Bros. Records|Warner Bros.]]' head of [[artists and repertoire|A&R]] – was in London looking for British material. When Joe heard Pet[ula]'s record, he loved it and scheduled the single for urgent release in the [United] States".<ref name="Going Back Downtown"/> When Hatch, surprised by Smith's enthusiasm for releasing "Downtown" in the US, asked if Smith didn't consider "Downtown" to be a "very English record" Smith replied: "It's perfect. It's just an observation from outside of America and it's just beautiful and just perfect."<ref name=retrosellers />

In the wake of Smith's interest, "Downtown" was released in the UK on 23 October 1964.<ref name=":0">{{Cite magazine |last=Anon. |date=19 December 1964 |title=Silver Discs for Matt, Val, Pet and Searchers |magazine=[[Disc (magazine)|Disc Weekly]] |page=4 |quote=Pet Clark's second Silver (her first was for "Sailor") was released on October 23.}}</ref> It entered the UK Top 50 dated 14 November 1964, ending a virtual two-year UK chart absence for Clark; of the ten singles she had released in the UK during that period only one, "[[I Will Follow Him|Chariot]]", had appeared in even the lower charts (No. 39 in early 1963). "Downtown" rose to No. 2 UK in December 1964, remaining there for three weeks, kept out of the No. 1 position by [[the Beatles]]' "[[I Feel Fine]]". Clark was awarded a [[Music recording certification|silver disc]] by [[Disc (magazine)|''Disc Weekly'']] for the sale of over 250,000 copies of "Downtown" in the UK.<ref name=":0" />

"Downtown" reached No. 2 in [[Irish Recorded Music Association|Ireland]] and No. 1 in Australia, New Zealand, Rhodesia and South Africa, and was also a hit in Denmark (No. 2), India (No. 3), the Netherlands (No. 4) and Norway (No. 8).

But "Downtown" had its greatest significance in the reception it was afforded in the United States, where it was released by Warner Bros. in November 1964: after early regional break-outs, notably in Detroit, Miami, and Washington D.C., "Downtown" debuted at No. 87 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|Hot 100]] chart in the ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' issue dated 19 December 1964. Despite the Christmas season typically being the worst time to break a new hit, "Downtown" shot up to No. 41 in its second week on the Hot 100 chart ascending in its third and fourth charting weeks to No. 12 and then No. 5; then after a subsequent single point advance to No. 4 "Downtown" leapt to No. 1 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 dated 23 January 1965, retaining that position a further week before being overtaken by the ascendancy of [[the Righteous Brothers]]' "[[You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin']]". The song became the first No. 1 hit for the year 1965.<ref name="Bronson">{{Cite book |title=The Billboard Book of Number 1 Hits |last=Bronson |first=Fred |author-link=Fred Bronson |year=2003 |publisher=Billboard Books |location=New York |isbn=0823076776 |page=165 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PgGqNrqfrsoC&pg=PT174 |access-date=8 July 2012 }}</ref>

Petula Clark thus became the first UK female artist to have a US No. 1 hit during the rock era and the second in the annals of US charted music, [[Vera Lynn]] having hit No. 1 in the US with "[[Auf Wiederseh'n Sweetheart]]" in 1952. "Downtown" also made Clark the first UK female artist to have a single certified as a [[RIAA certification|Gold record]] for US sales of one million units. On Billboard's annual Disk Jockey poll, "Downtown" was voted the second best single release of 1965 and Petula Clark was voted third most popular female vocalist.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eEUEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA58 |title= Billboard Magazine, March 1965|date= 27 March 1965|access-date=28 June 2018}}</ref> "Downtown" would be the first of fifteen consecutive hits Clark would place in the US Top 40 during a period when she had considerably less chart impact in her native UK, there reaching the Top 40 eight times.

Petula Clark, who had been playing to her French-speaking fans in small venues in Quebec when "Downtown" entered the US charts, swiftly cut non-English versions of the song for the markets in France, Italy and Germany; the absence in each region's language of a two-syllable equivalent of "downtown" necessitated a radical lyric recasting for the versions aimed at France ("Dans le temps"), Italy ("Ciao Ciao", winning the [[Festivalbar]], a juke-box contest) and Spain ("Chao Chao") which climbed the charts to No. 6, No. 2 and – for three weeks – No. 1; "Dans le temps" also reached No. 18 on Belgium's French-language chart. The title and lyric "Downtown" was retained for an otherwise German version which was the most successful foreign-language version, reaching No. 1 in Germany, No. 3 in Austria, and No. 11 on the charts for the Flemish region of Belgium. The Spanish version, however, was not recorded by Petula Clark herself but bis several Spanish artists, among them Gelu.

[[Mrs. Miller]] reached number 82 in the US with her version in 1966.

In 2013, Petula Clark re-recorded the song for her album ''Lost in You'', with new arrangements, as a ballad and with a soft voice, giving it a new life.

In the 1978 film ''[[Jaws 2]]'', as Police Chief Martin Brody enters the brand new [[Holiday Inn]] hotel prior to its grand opening ceremony on Amity Island, an instrumental version of the song (performed by the Amity High School Band) can be heard.

In the 1991 film ''[[Flight of the Intruder]]'', [[Brad Johnson (actor, born 1959)|Brad Johnson]] and [[Willem Dafoe]] sing the chorus portion of "Downtown" as they are flying their A-6 Intruder back to the aircraft carrier after the unauthorized bombing of the "Sam City" section of [[Hanoi]] in [[North Vietnam]].

In the 1993 [[Biographical film|biographical]] [[anthology film]] ''[[Thirty Two Short Films About Glenn Gould]]'', the song plays throughout "Truck Stop", the fifteenth segment.

In the 1996 ''[[Seinfeld]]'' episode "[[The Bottle Deposit]]", the song is referenced by [[George Costanza]]'s supervisor Wilhelm when discussing a project Costanza is in the dark about, prompting George Costanza and [[Jerry Seinfeld (character)|Jerry Seinfeld]] to analyze the song's lyrics for clues.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/tv/tv-lists/best-seinfeld-characters-soup-nazi-26801/jason-hanky-82823/ |title=From Soup Nazis to Nuts: 100 Best Seinfeld Characters |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |date=29 November 2020 |access-date=30 December 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=DeRogatis |first=Jim |title=Rolling with old gold - Reissues bring out best, and rest, of classic pop albums|newspaper=[[Chicago Sun-Times]] |date=27 February 2000 |page=15}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Top 10 TV musical moments of 2018 |url=https://www.michigandaily.com/section/bside/top-10-tv-shows |newspaper=[[The Michigan Daily]] |date=9 January 2019 |access-date=1 January 2021}}</ref>

The original 1964 recording was remixed and released in 1988 as "Downtown '88" which became a top ten UK hit.  The track also charted in Australia (No. 58),<ref name=aus89/> Belgium (Dutch chart No. 19), Finland (No. 3), Germany (No. 13) and Ireland (No. 14). Clark recalled: "The first time I heard the '88 remix of 'Downtown' I was in my car. I thought: 'This sounds familiar. I wonder who's singing this?' and it turned out to be me! They'd wiped out the orchestra and put on some kind of ticka-ticka-tick thing. I don't know what the hell it was, but it turned into a hit. They don't have to ask my permission, if you know what I mean. But it's fine. I find it rather flattering, actually. And quite amusing."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theage.com.au/articles/2004/03/11/1078594480628.html |title=The show must go on - Music |work=The Age |date=12 March 2004 |access-date=28 June 2017}}</ref>

Clark promoted "Downtown '88" in a live performance on 15 December 1988 broadcast of ''[[Top of the Pops]]'' (''TOTP'')<ref>{{cite web |author=TV.com |url=http://www.tv.com/shows/top-of-the-pops-uk/15th-december-1988-417500/ |title=Top of the Pops (UK) - Season 25, Episode 50: 15th December 1988 |publisher=TV.com |access-date=28 June 2017 |archive-date=14 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170914081722/http://www.tv.com/shows/top-of-the-pops-uk/15th-december-1988-417500/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> – the track had been aired on the preceding ''TOTP'' broadcast of 8 December 1988 and had moved from No. 37 to No. 24 on the UK Singles Chart dated (i.e. for the week ending) 12 December 1988: Clark's live ''TOTP'' performance evidently facilitated the rise of "Downtown '88" to No. 13 on the UK chart dated 17 December 1988, while the track reached its No. 10 peak on the UK chart dated 24 December 1988, that being the singles rankings for the first full week after Clark's ''TOTP'' live performance of "Downtown '88".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hardprog.pagesperso-orange.fr/top_of_the_pops_1988_episode_guide_2298.htm |title=top of the pops 1988 episode guide |publisher=Hardprog.pagesperso-orange.fr |access-date=28 June 2017}}</ref>

sections.heading: Other re-recordings
sections.wikitext: In October 2011, Clark recorded several lines of "Downtown" for inclusion in the remake by Irish band [[the Saw Doctors]] which was credited to the Saw Doctors featuring Petula Clark – [[#Saw Doctors version|(see below)]]. Clark's own 2013 album release ''Lost in You'' features a new version of "Downtown": Clark said she was uninterested when it was first suggested she again record "Downtown", then "I was played this beautiful [instrumental] track ...And I said it was lovely, and they told me it was [intended for] 'Downtown.' I got to the microphone and I didn't know how I was going to sing it, and it really feels like a new song."<ref>{{cite web|author=Michael Cragg |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2013/feb/20/30-minutes-with-petula-clark |title=Petula Clark: 'John Lennon gave me some advice that I can't repeat'|work=The Guardian|date=20 February 2013 |access-date=14 June 2014}}</ref> Reviewing ''Lost in You'' for MusicOHM.com, Philip Matusavage writes of the "Downtown" remake: "already a song loaded with melancholy, the stately version here acquires new meaning with its weary but amiable delivery summoning forth powerful nostalgia and the sense of someone fondly remembering their youth."<ref>{{cite web|last=Matusavage |first=Philip |url=http://www.musicomh.com/reviews/albums/petula-clark-lost-in-you |title=Petula Clark – Lost in You | Album Reviews |work=musicOMH |date=20 February 2013 |access-date=14 June 2014}}</ref>

[[Dolly Parton]] recorded "Downtown" in [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] in 1983 in the sessions for her [[Covers albums|covers album]]  ''[[The Great Pretender (Dolly Parton album)|The Great Pretender]]'', a [[Val Garay]] production which focused on hits from the 1950s and 1960s. "Downtown" served as the album's second single release in March 1984 reaching No. 36 on the [[Hot Country Songs|''Billboard'' C&W chart]] and [[crossover (music)|crossing over]] to No. 80 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 pop chart: to date "Downtown" marks Parton's final solo Hot 100 appearance. Parton's version altered some of the lyrics: "Listen to the rhythm of a gentle [[bossa nova]]" became "Listen to the rhythm of the music that they're playing". Petula Clark has described Parton's take on "Downtown" as "cute, because she didn't even try to sound like my recording."<ref name="Star Observer">{{cite web|url=http://www.starobserver.com.au/features/entertainment-features/entertainment-play/2010/09/07/petula-still-on-song-at-77/30446|title=Star Observer|date=7 September 2010|publisher=Starobserver.com.au|access-date=14 June 2014}}</ref>

Dolly Parton recorded "Downtown" in Nashville in 1983 in the sessions for her covers album  The Great Pretender, a Val Garay production which focused on hits from the 1950s and 1960s. "Downtown" served as the album's second single release in March 1984 reaching No. 36 on the Billboard C&W chart and crossing over to No. 80 on the Billboard Hot 100 pop chart: to date "Downtown" marks Parton's final solo Hot 100 appearance. Parton's version altered some of the lyrics: "Listen to the rhythm of a gentle bossa nova" became "Listen to the rhythm of the music that they're playing". Petula Clark has described Parton's take on "Downtown" as "cute, because she didn't even try to sound like my recording."

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
[[BBC News]] announced 20 October 2006 that [[Emma Bunton]] would record a remake of the [[Petula Clark]] hit "Downtown" to be the 2006 official BBC [[Children in Need]] single, with Bunton quoted as saying: "I've always loved 'Downtown'<small>...</small>and I'm really looking forward to putting my own stamp on it. The track's good fun and one everyone will know."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/6069004.stm |title=Entertainment | Bunton sings for Children in Need |work=BBC News |date=20 October 2006 |access-date=14 June 2014}}</ref> Bunton, whose admiration for Petula Clark was evident on the 2004 ''[[Free Me (album)|Free Me]]'' album, recorded "Downtown" at [[Air Lyndhurst|AIR Studios]]' Lyndhurst Hall location with Simon Franglen producing; the orchestra for the track was recorded at [[Angel Recording Studios]] with Gavin Wright conducting. The track was released on 13 November 2006 and Bunton premiered her version of "Downtown" on the 2006 ''Children in Need'' telethon which began broadcast 17 November 2006.

Although Bunton said that she knew "Downtown" composer [[Tony Hatch]] "quite well",<ref name="Emma Bunton Interview">{{cite web| last = Baggs | first = Michael | date = 6 December 2006 | title = Emma Bunton interview | work = [[Popjustice]] | access-date = 13 February 2013 | url = http://www.popjustice.com/interviewsandfeatures/emma-bunton-interview/49818/}}</ref> Petula Clark said that neither she [i.e. Clark] nor Hatch had prior knowledge of Bunton's remake.<ref name="Contact Music">{{cite web|url=http://www.contactmusic.com/news/clark-gives-bunton-her-blessing_1016647|title=Contact Music|publisher=Contactmusic.com|access-date=14 June 2014}}</ref> Clark also stated that she considered Bunton's remake to be an "outright copy"<ref name="Star Observer"/> of Clark's original recording: "I could ask: 'What's the point'<small>...</small>but Emma's recording is wonderful and<small>...</small>for a great cause"<ref name="Contact Music"/> (i.e. Children in Need).

sections.heading: Impact
sections.wikitext:
"Downtown" by Emma Bunton debuted on the UK singles chart 25 November 2006 at No. 24. [[Central FM (Spanish radio station)|Central FM]] noted Bunton's chart debut, declaring "Downtown" "the song she was born to cover<small>...</small>One of the all time great pop songs, ['Downtown'] was long overdue for a revival and Emma Bunton pays it the respect it deserves." The Spanish radio station predicted "Downtown" would rise to the Top 3 in its second week and the single did indeed jump to No. 3 on the chart for 2 December 2006 having sold 30,582 units in the relevant week: the mid-week stats had ranked "Downtown" at No. 2 behind "[[Patience (Take That song)|Patience]]" by [[Take That]] but on the chart for the full week Bunton was bested not only by Take That at No. 1 but by the previous week's No. 1, "[[Smack That]]" by [[Akon]], which outsold "Downtown" by 57 copies.<ref>Musicweek.com 27 November 2006</ref>

Total UK sales for "Downtown" by Emma Bunton were at 83,000 units.

sections.heading: Saw Doctors version
sections.wikitext:
In October 2011, Irish band [[the Saw Doctors]] remade "Downtown" with Petula Clark singing some lines: the track is credited to the Saw Doctors featuring Petula Clark. According to Saw Doctors' member [[Leo Moran]] the group habitually played snippets of well-known songs during their encore numbers: "One night for no particular reason we did 'Downtown' and you could see people loved it. All ages. You could see it brought joy to people's faces."<ref name="Worcester Telegram">Worcester Telegram 1 March 2012 "Saw Doctors Headed to The Hanover Theatre"</ref> Some time later the Saw Doctors learned their producer Philip Tennant was friends with Petula Clark's manager John Williams and an invitation was conveyed to Clark to sing on a Saw Doctors' remake of "Downtown"; Clark being agreeable, a session was booked in a London recording studio to allow the Irish group to liaison with the European-based Clark and "Downtown" was recorded over two days with Clark arriving to record her vocal on the second day. Moran recalls: "We [the Saw Doctors] did a whole lot of work the first day. [Petula Clark] came in the second evening and we discovered that the song was in the wrong key. So we had to scrap all of the first day's work and put down the backing track with Petula because she only had a few hours that evening and wasn't able to come back the following day. It was exciting, exhilarating, scary and privileged … rolled into one."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pollstar.com/news_article.aspx?ID=801008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140601003714/http://www.pollstar.com/news_article.aspx?ID=801008 |url-status=dead |archive-date=1 June 2014 |title=Saw Doctors' Leo Moran on Music, Touring & Everything |publisher=Pollstar |access-date=14 June 2014}}</ref>

Top Irish [[cinematographer]] Eugene O' Connor (''[[Father Ted]]'') directed the video for the Saw Doctor's "Downtown" which was uploaded to YouTube on 17 November 2011. Shot on the nights of 9–10 November 2011, the video focuses on the band's members walking through the town center of [[Galway]] (lead vocalist [[Davy Carton]] is also seen briefly riding in a car). Footage of Clark was shot in Paris and spliced into the completed video in which she mainly appears on the screens of [[television set|televisions]] displayed in a shop window (the shop is in fact clothing retailer Anthony Ryans) outside of which the Saw Doctors perform on the street in the company of eight members of the Galway City Cougars [[cheerleading]] squad and also a [[torch (juggling)|fire juggler]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.stuntworxelite.com/cheerleading.html |title=Cheerleading - Stuntworx Cheer & Trampoline |access-date=28 June 2017 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160816025101/http://www.stuntworxelite.com/cheerleading.html |archive-date=16 August 2016}}</ref>

Radio presenter [[Ray Foley]] ([[Today FM]]) began a campaign to make the Saw Doctors' "Downtown" the Christmas No. 1 in Ireland for 2011 encouraging sales of the track upon its 16 December 2011 release with the intent of propelling it to the No. 1 position on the Irish Singles Chart for the week ending 22 December 2011 and the Saw Doctors' "Downtown" was indeed No. 1 on [[iTunes Store|iTunes]] Ireland for the relevant period. However, on the Irish Singles Chart dated 22 December 2011 the track debuted at No. 2 with "[[Cannonball (Damien Rice song)|Cannonball]]" by [[Little Mix]] retaining the No. 1 position largely because of "Cannonball"'s greater availability as a CD single – 10,000 units as opposed to "Downtown"'s 2000 – making "Cannonball" a more attractive prospect for gift-buyers.<ref>{{cite news|author=Independent Woman |url=http://www.independent.ie/entertainment/music/saw-doctors-leave-n17-for-downtown-2933643.html |title=Saw Doctors leave N17 for 'Downtown' – Music, Entertainment |work=The Irish Independent |date= 14 November 2011|access-date=5 January 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Sligo bay |url=http://www.independent.ie/entertainment/music/cannonball-hits-saw-docs-no-1-hope-2969490.html |title=Cannonball hits Saw Docs' No 1 hope – Music, Entertainment |work=The Irish Independent |date= 21 December 2011|access-date=5 January 2012}}</ref><ref name="IRMA">{{cite web|url=http://irma.ie/aucharts.asp |title=IRMA : Irish Charts - Singles, Albums & Compilations |publisher=Irma.ie |date=29 December 2011 |access-date=5 January 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120511020134/http://irma.ie/aucharts.asp |archive-date=11 May 2012}}</ref>

On the Irish Singles Chart dated 29 December 2011 "Downtown" by the Saw Doctors featuring Petula Clark was ranked at No. 43 in its second and final week on the chart.<ref name="IRMA"/>
